tracks.name: Unit Tests
tracks.description: Test functions in isolation, including the awkward inputs.

lessons.title: 1. Your first test
lessons.summary: Arrange the input, act, then assert on the result.

activities.title: One behaviour per test
activities.instruction: `describe` groups related tests, `it` states one behaviour, and `expect` asserts. A failing test should tell you which behaviour broke without opening the source.

activities.title: Naming tests
activities.question: Which test name gives the most useful failure message?
activities.explanation: The name should describe the behaviour. A failure then reads as a sentence: `addToCart › rejects a quantity of zero`.

activities.title: Test a function
activities.instruction: Write a `describe` containing one `it` that calls `addToCart([], item)` and asserts the cart has length 1.

teaching.text: Tests are executable documentation. Each one sets up a state, calls the code, and asserts on the outcome.
A test with several unrelated assertions hides which one failed. Split it, or use `it.each` for the same assertion over many inputs.

lessons.task: Write a describe/it test for addToCart.
lessons.starterCode:
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';

// Test addToCart
hints: You need a description, a callback, and at least one assertion.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What does a good failure message tell you before you open the source file?

lessons.title: 2. Edge cases
lessons.summary: Feed the same assertion a table of inputs, including the ugly ones.

activities.title: The table is the spec
activities.instruction: Loop over cases and assert on each. Empty input, one item, duplicates, and the maximum all belong in the table — those are where bugs live.

activities.title: Happy path only
activities.question: Every test uses a cart with at least one item. What class of bug gets through?
choices: Empty-input and boundary bugs, which are the common ones
activities.answer: Empty-input and boundary bugs, which are the common ones
activities.explanation: Real bugs cluster at zero, one, maximum, and malformed input. A test suite that only exercises the normal path misses them.

activities.title: Table of cases
activities.instruction: Write a cases array with an empty cart and a one-item cart, then assert each with `forEach`.

teaching.text: A table-driven test keeps the assertion fixed and varies the input. Adding a case is one line, which is why people actually add them.
Include the empty case explicitly. `reduce` without an initial value throws on an empty array — that bug ships constantly.

lessons.task: Test an empty cart and a one-item cart from a cases array.
hints: Each case needs an input and an expected total.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which boundary values would you add for a function that paginates a list?

lessons.title: 3. Mocking a dependency
lessons.summary: Replace the database so a unit test stays fast and deterministic.

activities.title: Stub the boundary
activities.instruction: Mock the module at the edge of your code, not the function under test. `mockResolvedValue` makes an async dependency resolve to a fixed value.

activities.title: Mocking too much
activities.question: A test mocks the function it is supposed to be testing. What does it prove?
choices: Nothing — the assertion now tests the mock
activities.answer: Nothing — the assertion now tests the mock
activities.explanation: Mock the boundary (database, HTTP, clock) and assert on your own code's behaviour through it.

activities.title: Mock the database
activities.instruction: Mock `./db.js` with a `findById` mock and make it resolve to null in a test.

teaching.text: Mocks remove the slow, flaky parts: network, database, filesystem, time. They also let you test the failure paths you cannot trigger against a real service.
Clear mocks between tests (`vi.clearAllMocks()` or `clearMocks: true`). A leftover `mockResolvedValue` is a classic order-dependent failure.

lessons.task: Mock the db module and make findById resolve to null.
hints: The factory returns the module shape you need.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does mocking the function under test make a green suite worthless?

lessons.title: 4. Choosing an assertion
lessons.summary: The wrong matcher turns a real failure into a pass.

activities.title: Same shape, different check
activities.instruction: `toBe` compares identity — fine for primitives, wrong for objects. `toEqual` compares structure. `toThrow` checks that a call fails, optionally with a message.

activities.title: toBe on objects
activities.question: `expect({ a: 1 }).toBe({ a: 1 })` — does it pass?
choices: No — they are two different objects
activities.answer: No — they are two different objects
activities.explanation: `toBe` uses Object.is. Two literals are distinct references, so use `toEqual` for structure.

activities.title: Match the value and the throw
activities.instruction: Assert that `parseOrder({ id: 1 })` deep-equals `{ id: 1, items: [] }`, and that `parseOrder(null)` throws.

teaching.text: Matchers encode intent. `toEqual` for data, `toBe` for identity, `toBeCloseTo` for floats, `toThrow` for errors.

expect(parseOrder({ id: 1 })).toEqual({ id: 1, items: [] });
expect(() => parseOrder(null)).toThrow('order must be an object');
Pass a function to `toThrow`, not the result: `expect(fn())` runs the throw before the assertion and fails the test differently.

lessons.task: Use toEqual for the result and toThrow for invalid input.
hints: Wrap the throwing call in an arrow function.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does `expect(fn())` fail to test a thrown error the way `expect(() => fn())` does?

tracks.name: API Tests
tracks.description: Exercise real routes without starting a server by hand.

lessons.title: 5. Testing a route
lessons.summary: Send a request to the app object and read the response.

activities.title: No port needed
activities.instruction: `request(app)` starts an ephemeral server for the request and closes it. That keeps tests parallel-safe, unlike binding port 3000 in every worker.

activities.title: Why not listen()
activities.question: Why should tests import the app without calling `app.listen()`?
choices: Two test files would fight over the same port
Supertest cannot reach a listening server
activities.answer: Two test files would fight over the same port
activities.explanation: Supertest handles the socket for you. Hard-coding a port makes parallel runs conflict and leaves handles open.

activities.title: Call the health route
activities.instruction: Write a test that GETs `/health` with supertest and expects status 200.

teaching.text: API tests are the sweet spot for a full-stack app: they exercise routing, middleware, validation, and serialization without a browser.

const res = await request(app).get('/health');
expect(res.status).toBe(200);
Export the app from a module and start the server in a separate entry file. Importing a file that listens opens a port as a side effect.

hints: `request(app).get(path)` returns a thenable, so await it.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What does an API test cover that a unit test of the handler function does not?

lessons.title: 6. Status and body
lessons.summary: A route can be right about the status and wrong about the payload.

activities.title: Assert the contract
activities.instruction: Check the status, then the fields the client depends on. Asserting the whole object is brittle; asserting `id` and `name` catches real regressions.

activities.title: Brittle assertion
activities.question: Why is `expect(res.body).toEqual(exactFixture)` fragile?
choices: Any harmless new field breaks the test
activities.answer: Any harmless new field breaks the test
activities.explanation: Assert the fields the client relies on. Whole-object snapshots turn additive changes into failing tests.

activities.title: Assert the created product
activities.instruction: POST `{ name: 'Keyboard' }` to `/products`, expect 201, and assert the body has that name and a defined id.

teaching.text: The response body is your API's contract. Test the parts clients read, plus the status codes they branch on.
Also test the error shape once: 400 with `{ error }`. Clients switch on it, and it silently changes when validation moves.

lessons.task: Assert the POST /products status and body.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is asserting two fields better than asserting the entire response object?

lessons.title: 7. Database setup and teardown
lessons.summary: Every test should start from a known database state.

activities.title: Clean slate per test
activities.instruction: `beforeEach` resets the data before each test, and `afterAll` closes the pool so the process can exit. Shared state between tests creates failures that depend on order.

activities.title: Leaked connections
activities.question: Tests pass but the run hangs after the last file. What is the usual cause?
choices: An open database or server handle that is never closed
activities.answer: An open database or server handle that is never closed
activities.explanation: Node exits when the event loop is empty. An open connection pool keeps it alive; close it in `afterAll`.

activities.title: Reset and clean up
activities.instruction: Add a `beforeEach` that clears the products collection and an `afterAll` that closes the client.

teaching.text: Tests must not depend on each other. Resetting state before each test costs milliseconds and removes whole classes of flakiness.
Never point the test suite at your development database. A mis-scoped `deleteMany({})` would erase real work.

lessons.task: Reset the collection before each test and close the client after all.
lessons.starterCode: // Set up and tear down the database
hints: Hooks are async — await the cleanup inside them.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can tests pass individually but fail when the whole suite runs in a different order?

lessons.title: 8. Testing protected routes
lessons.summary: Requests need credentials, and the rejection path needs a test too.

activities.title: Sign in, then call
activities.instruction: Get a token from the login route (or sign one in the test), attach it with `.set('Authorization', \`Bearer ${token}\`)`, and call the protected route.

activities.title: Missing test
activities.question: Which case is most often forgotten in protected-route tests?
choices: The request with no token, which must return 401
activities.answer: The request with no token, which must return 401
activities.explanation: The happy path is easy to remember. The unauthenticated case is the security property, so it needs its own test.

activities.title: Attach a token
activities.instruction: Call GET `/orders` with a Bearer token from `login.body.token` and expect 200.

teaching.text: Auth tests should cover three requests: no credentials, valid credentials, and insufficient permission. Each maps to a different status.
Sign test tokens with the test secret and short expiry. Never reuse a real user's credentials in the suite.

lessons.task: Test a protected route with a Bearer token.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is the unauthenticated request the most important case to test on a protected route?

tracks.name: End-to-End
tracks.description: Drive the real app in a real browser like a user would.

lessons.title: 9. Your first browser test
lessons.summary: Playwright launches a browser, navigates, and waits for assertions.

activities.title: A real browser
activities.instruction: `page.goto` navigates, and `await expect(locator)` retries until it passes or times out. That auto-waiting is why Playwright tests rarely need sleeps.

activities.title: Why no sleep
activities.question: Why does `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()` beat `await page.waitForTimeout(1000)`?
choices: It retries until the condition holds, and fails fast instead of always waiting a second
activities.answer: It retries until the condition holds, and fails fast instead of always waiting a second
activities.explanation: Fixed sleeps make suites slow and still flaky. Web-first assertions poll and fail with a useful message.

activities.title: Load the home page
activities.instruction: Write a test that goes to `/` and asserts the heading 'Welcome' is visible.

teaching.text: E2E tests are slow and valuable: they prove the assembled app works in a browser, including routing, forms, and auth.

await page.goto('/');
await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Welcome' })).toBeVisible();
Keep the E2E set small and focused on critical journeys. Everything below that belongs in an API or unit test, where failures are cheaper to diagnose.

lessons.task: Visit / and assert the Welcome heading is visible.
lessons.starterCode:
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Load the home page
hints: The test receives `{ page }` as a fixture.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which user journeys deserve an E2E test when each one costs seconds per run?

lessons.title: 10. Locators and actions
lessons.summary: Query the way a user perceives the page, not by CSS class.

activities.title: Accessible names first
activities.instruction: `getByRole` finds elements by the role and label assistive tech sees. `.fill` types into a field and `.click` activates a control. Both auto-wait for the element to be actionable.

activities.title: CSS selectors
activities.question: Why avoid `page.locator('.btn-primary:nth-child(2)')`?
choices: It breaks on styling or layout changes that do not affect behaviour
activities.answer: It breaks on styling or layout changes that do not affect behaviour
activities.explanation: Role and label locators describe what the user sees. Class and position selectors couple the test to the implementation.

activities.title: Fill the login form
activities.instruction: Click the 'Sign in' link, fill the Email and Password fields, and click the 'Log in' button.

teaching.text: Locators that mirror the accessible tree also push you toward a more accessible UI — a useful side effect.

await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('a@b.c');
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log in' }).click();
If a control is hard to locate by role or label, that usually means a screen-reader user cannot find it either.

lessons.task: Fill the login form using role and label locators.
hints: `getByLabel` matches the label text associated with an input.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a button without an accessible name make a Playwright test harder to write?

lessons.title: 11. Testing the whole journey
lessons.summary: One test walks signup to a signed-in page and checks the URL.

activities.title: Assert where the user landed
activities.instruction: After submitting, assert the URL and something only a signed-in user can see. Checking the URL alone can pass while the page is still an error screen.

activities.title: URL only
activities.question: The URL becomes /dashboard but the page shows "Unauthorized". Would a URL-only assertion catch it?
choices: No — assert visible content as well
activities.answer: No — assert visible content as well
activities.explanation: Client-side routing can change the URL before data arrives or after an auth failure. Assert what the user sees.

activities.title: Login journey
activities.instruction: Submit the login form, then assert the URL is `/dashboard` and the 'Dashboard' heading is visible.

teaching.text: The login journey covers the most integration points in one test: form, API, cookie, session, redirect, and protected render.

await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
Seed the test user through the API or a fixture, not the signup form. That keeps this test about logging in.

lessons.task: Test login through to the dashboard.
lessons.starterCode: // Log in and land on the dashboard
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should this test start from a seeded user rather than signing up through the UI?

lessons.title: 12. Running in CI
lessons.summary: Tests only protect you if they run on every push.

activities.title: One workflow, every push
activities.instruction: A workflow checks out the code, installs dependencies, installs browsers, and runs the suite. `npm ci` plus a lockfile makes the run reproducible.
activities.example:
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test

activities.title: Uploading failures
activities.question: Why upload the Playwright report as an artifact on failure?
choices: Traces and screenshots explain a failure you cannot reproduce locally
activities.answer: Traces and screenshots explain a failure you cannot reproduce locally
activities.explanation: A trace records DOM snapshots and network calls per step, which is usually enough to diagnose a flaky CI failure without re-running.

activities.title: Add the workflow
activities.instruction: Write a workflow triggered on push that checks out the code, runs `npm ci`, and runs `npx playwright test`.

teaching.text: CI is the enforcement point: tests, type checks, and builds run on a clean machine before anything merges.

on: [push, pull_request]
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - run: npm ci
  - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
  - run: npx playwright test
Start the app for E2E tests through `webServer` in the Playwright config. A manually started server is the most common source of CI-only failures.

lessons.task: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that installs deps and runs Playwright.
hints: Start with `on: [push, pull_request]` and a `jobs:` block.
lessons.solution:
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does `npm ci` make CI runs more reproducible than `npm install`?
